content: Individuals may be provided with tuberculosis (TB) preventive treatment following an evaluation or in accordance with national guidelines. For certain high-risk household contacts of patients with multidrug-resistant TB, preventive treatment can be considered based on a personalized risk assessment and strong clinical justification. Patients initiating anti-TNF treatment, those undergoing dialysis, individuals preparing for organ or hematological transplants, and patients with silicosis should be systematically tested and treated for latent TB infection (LTBI). Additionally, systematic LTBI testing and treatment may be considered for prisoners, healthcare workers, immigrants from countries with a high TB burden, homeless individuals, and people who use drugs. However, systematic LTBI testing and treatment are not recommended for individuals with diabetes, those who engage in harmful alcohol use, tobacco smokers, or underweight individuals unless they belong to other high-risk groups identified in the recommendations. Adults and adolescents living with HIV should be screened for TB using a clinical algorithm. Those without symptoms such as current cough, fever, weight loss, or night sweats are unlikely to have active TB and should be offered preventive treatment regardless of their antiretroviral therapy (ART) status. Conversely, individuals reporting any of these symptoms should be evaluated for TB and other diseases, and if active TB is excluded, they should be offered preventive treatment. Chest radiography may be used to rule out active TB in people living with HIV on ART, and preventive treatment should be provided to those with no abnormal radiographic findings. Infants and children living with HIV who exhibit poor weight gain, fever, current cough, or have a history of contact with a TB case should be evaluated for TB and other diseases causing these symptoms. If active TB is excluded after appropriate clinical evaluation or in line with national guidelines, these children should be offered TB preventive treatment regardless of their age. Among HIV-negative household contacts aged 5 years or older and other risk groups, the absence of TB symptoms and normal chest radiographic findings can be used to rule out active TB before initiating preventive treatment. Testing for LTBI can be performed using either a tuberculin skin test (TST) or an interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA). However, LTBI testing is not a prerequisite for initiating preventive treatment in people living with HIV or child household contacts under 5 years of age. For LTBI treatment, the following regimens are recommended regardless of HIV status: 6 or 9 months of daily isoniazid, a 3-month regimen of weekly rifapentine plus isoniazid, or a 3-month regimen of daily isoniazid plus rifampicin. Alternative options include a 1-month regimen of daily rifapentine plus isoniazid or 4 months of daily rifampicin alone. For children and adolescents under 15 years in high TB incidence countries, a 3-month regimen of daily isoniazid plus rifampicin is recommended as an alternative to 6 months of isoniazid monotherapy. Similarly, a 3-month regimen of weekly rifapentine and isoniazid may be offered as an alternative to 6 months of isoniazid monotherapy for both adults and children in high TB incidence countries. In settings with high TB transmission, adults and adolescents living with HIV who have an unknown or positive LTBI test and are unlikely to have active TB disease should receive at least 36 months of daily isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT). This should be provided regardless of ART status, degree of immunosuppression, history of previous TB treatment, or pregnancy. National authorities define high TB transmission settings, and IPT should be implemented accordingly.
